title: {{NAME}} and the Wilderness Response Team
moral: Heroism is not always visible, but it is always felt by those who needed it.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a dark green rescue hero suit with amber sensor panels, dark boots, and amber gloves — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}}'s hero name was Ranger, and his team operated in places no other hero would go: the places without people, where the emergencies were wild and the victims couldn't report them.

His team: himself, SCOUT (a robot with advanced terrain navigation), and a network of animal contacts built over two years.

The crow network alone had saved three operations: crows remembered faces and locations with extraordinary precision and would lead him to the right spot every time.

Today: a distress call from the crow network. Unknown nature. High meadow. Go now.

No text, no words, no letters anywhere in the image.

pages.content:
The problem: a young brown bear had gotten its back leg tangled in old fencing wire, embedded in overgrown bracken. It had been there at least a day.

The bear was exhausted and frightened. SCOUT scanned the wire configuration and calculated the safest removal sequence.

The crow network had positioned two large ravens nearby to call if anyone approached.

{{NAME}} crouched down and said, in his steadiest voice: "I see what happened. I know how to fix it. It will take ten minutes. I need you to stay still."

The bear looked at him.

Then it went still.

No text, no words, no letters anywhere in the image.

pages.content:
SCOUT guided each cut with its analysis: this wire first, angle here, not that one yet.

{{NAME}} worked slowly and precisely, talking to the bear throughout, his voice steady and low.

With the fifth cut, the last wire came free.

The bear lay still for a moment, then slowly pulled its leg toward itself and tested it.

Weighted. Stood.

Walked three steps.

{{NAME}} sat back on his heels and let his breath out.

SCOUT's status light: green.

pages.content:
The bear stood for a long moment at the meadow edge.

It looked back at {{NAME}} once: a deep look, the kind that animals give when they have understood something about you.

Then it was gone into the treeline.

{{NAME}} sat in the meadow with SCOUT and the crows for a while after.

He radioed the operation in: "Bear free and mobile. Wire removed. No further assistance required."

"Good work, Ranger."

"Whole team," he said. "SCOUT and the crow network, specifically. Put them in the report."

pages.content:
He walked back down the mountain in the long evening light.

The crows flew with him to the treeline, then peeled away.

SCOUT rolled beside him in silent efficient mode.

At the road, {{NAME}} stopped and looked back up at the meadow, already small and unreachable.

He thought: up there, right now, a bear is walking on a leg that works.

He climbed in the truck.

In bed that night, SCOUT in the back room, the crow network somewhere in the dark trees, he fell asleep to the sound of a world that was, right now, slightly better than it had been this morning.
